options.text: An open ecosystem exchanges both energy and matter with its surroundings.
A closed ecosystem exchanges both energy and matter with its surroundings.
A closed ecosystem exchanges only matter and no energy with its surroundings.
An open ecosystem exchanges only energy and no matter with its surroundings.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**An open ecosystem exchanges both energy and matter with its surroundings.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• An ecosystem is a complex network of living organisms, their physical environment, and the interactions between them.
 
• The ecosystem can either be an open system or a closed system.
 
• .An open system is a system that can exchange both matter and energy with its surroundings.
 
• In an open ecosystem, there is a continuous exchange of matter and energy between the biotic and abiotic components of the ecosystem and the surrounding environment.
 
• This exchange of matter and energy is crucial for the survival of the organisms in the ecosystem.
 
• Examples of open ecosystems include forests, grasslands, and oceans.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Closed Ecosystem:**

 
 
• ​A closed system is a system that can exchange energy but not matter with its surroundings.
 
• In a closed ecosystem, there is no exchange of matter with the surrounding environment.
 
• The matter within the ecosystem is recycled and reused, and there are no inputs or outputs of matter.
 
• Energy, on the other hand, can enter and leave the ecosystem.
 
• An example of a closed ecosystem is a terrarium or an aquarium.

questions.question: In which of the following cases has the Supreme Court of India opined that the Constitution of India is founded on the bedrock of the balance between the Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Minerva Mills Case**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Supreme Court, in the Minerva Mills Case, opined that the Constitution of India is founded on the bedrock of the balance between the Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy.
 
• This landmark judgment emphasized that neither Fundamental Rights nor Directive Principles can override one another.
 
• The balance and harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution.
 
• This judgment was delivered on 31st July 1980 and is considered a crucial ruling in maintaining the basic structure doctrine established in the Keshvananda Bharati Case.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Keshvananda Bharati Case (1973)**

 
 
• This landmark case established the basic structure doctrine, declaring that the basic structure of the Constitution cannot be altered by any amendment.
 
• The case was a challenge to the 24th Amendment of the Indian Constitution, where the Supreme Court held that Parliament could amend any part of the Constitution but not its basic structure.
 
 
 
• **Golaknath Case (1967)**
 
 
• This case ruled that Parliament could not curtail any of the Fundamental Rights guaranteed under the Constitution.
 
• The decision was later overturned by the 24th Amendment.
 
 
 
• **Maneka Gandhi Case (1978)**
 
 
• This case extended the interpretation of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.
 
• The judgment emphasized the importance of due process of law and widened the scope of Article 21 by including various rights under it.
 
 
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy**
 
 
• These are guidelines to the central and state governments of India, to be kept in mind while framing laws and policies.
 
• They are not justiciable, meaning they are not enforceable by any court, but they are considered fundamental in the governance of the country.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights**
 
 
• These are a set of rights granted to the citizens of India under Part III of the Constitution.
 
• They are enforceable by the courts and include rights such as the right to equality, freedom, religion, cultural and educational rights, etc.

questions.question: Biodiversity is defined as a:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is the __**wide variety of living organisms.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Biodiversity

 
 
• Biodiversity is the variety of life found in a place on Earth or, often, the total variety of life on Earth.
 
• A common measure of this variety, called species richness, is the count of species in an area.
 
• Colombia and Kenya, for example, each have more than 1,000 breeding species of birds, whereas the forests of Great Britain and eastern North America are home to fewer than 200.
 
• A coral reef off northern Australia may have 500 species of fish, while the rocky shoreline of Japan may be home to only 100 species.
 
• Such numbers capture some of the differences between places—the tropics, for example, have more biodiversity than temperate regions—but raw species count is not the only measure of diversity.
 
• Furthermore, biodiversity encompasses the genetic variety within each species and the variety of ecosystems that species create.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Measuring biodiversity

 
• Although examining counts of species is perhaps the most common method used to compare the biodiversity of various places.
 
• Biodiversity is weighted differently for different species, the reason being that some species are deemed more valuable or more interesting than others.
 
• One way this value or interest is assessed is by examining the diversity that exists above the species level, in the genera, families, orders, classes, and phyla to which species belong.
 
• For example, the count of animal species that live on land is much higher than the count of those that live in the oceans because there are huge numbers of terrestrial insect species, insects comprise many orders and families, and they constitute the largest class of arthropods, which themselves constitute the largest animal phylum.
 
• In contrast, there are fewer animal phyla in terrestrial environments than in the oceans.
 
• No animal phylum is restricted to the land, but brachiopods, pogonophorans, and other animal phyla occur exclusively or predominantly in marine habitats.

questions.question: While Proclamation of emergency is in operation, the term of the Lok Sabha can be extended for a period not exceeding ___________________at a time.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**one year**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• While a proclamation of emergency is in operation the duration of the Lok Sabha can be extended for a period not exceeding more than one year at a time.
 
• The effect of this emergency is that while it is in operation, the life of Lok Sabha may be extended beyond its normal term i.e., beyond five years by a law of Parliament.
 
• It **can be extended for one year at a time** and cannot be continued beyond six months if the emergency has ceased to operate or revoked. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Proclamation of Emergency**

 
 
• Under **Article 352**, the President can issue a proclamation of National emergency on the grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.
 
• President can declare emergency rule in the whole of India or on any part of the Indian Territory.
 
• This is also called a ‘National Emergency’.
 
• The effect of this emergency is that while it is in operation, the life of Lok Sabha may be extended beyond its normal term i.e., beyond five years by a law of Parliament.
 
• It can be extended for one year at a time and cannot be continued beyond six months if the emergency has ceased to operate or revoked.

questions.question: Which of the following risks, with reference to the usage of technology during green revolution, was significantly reduced by the services provided by the research institutes established by the government?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pest attacks**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The Green Revolution, initiated in the 1960s, greatly increased agricultural production in India through the adoption of modern methods and technology, such as the use of **high-yielding variety (HYV) of seeds, increased use of fertilizers, irrigation, and mechanization**.
 
• With the introduction of these new agricultural technologies and practices, the risk of pest attacks also increased as monoculture (cultivation of a single crop in a given area) could attract specific pests.
 
• However, government-established research institutes played a vital role in reducing this risk.
 
• Institutions like the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) and state agricultural universities have been instrumental in **creating and promoting integrated pest management strategies, training for farmers, and developing pest-resistant varieties of major crops. Hence, option 4 is correct.**
 
• The Green Revolution technology was mainly adopted in the areas where irrigation facilities were available, **leading to an increase in regional disparities**. The increase in agricultural productivity was more noticeable in Punjab, Haryana, and Western Uttar Pradesh compared to other states in the country.
 
• The Green Revolution **led to inter-crop imbalances as it was more focused on wheat and rice**. The production of these two grains increased significantly but the output of other grains like pulses and millets did not see substantial growth.
 
• There was an **increase in income inequalities** during the Green Revolution. The wealthier farmers who could afford the new technology made huge profits, while poor farmers who couldn't afford the technology did not benefit. The** gap between the rich and poor farmers thus widened causing income disparities**.

questions.question: In which year was India’s first paperless budget presented in the Parliament?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is__** 2021**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **India's first paperless budget was presented by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on February 1, 2021.**
 
• Owing to the COVID-19 pandemic,** the traditional 'budget bahi khata' was replaced by a 'Made in India' tablet.**
 
• The tradition of presenting a paperless budget in the Parliament was initiated in 2021, in light of the coronavirus pandemic and as a measure of digital progression.
 
• This marked a significant step in the ongoing digital revolution and was seen as an effort towards creating a more sustainable and environmentally friendly workflow within the government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Union Budget of a country is a comprehensive **annual financial statement** outlining the government's estimated revenue from taxes and expenditures for the forthcoming fiscal year.
 
• It details the financial plan involving two main components: **revenue and expenditure.**
 
• The revenue budget includes tax income and other types of revenue, while the expenditure budget is the estimate of total spending, categorized into plan (for growth, development, and welfare measures) and non-plan expenditures (for the everyday running of state departments).

• The** Union List** includes subjects on which** only the Parliament** can make laws.
 
• The **State List** includes subjects on which** only the** **State Legislatures** can make laws.
 
• The** Concurrent List** includes subjects on which **both the Parliament and State Legislatures** can make laws, but if there is a conflict, the **Union law prevails**.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment?

• Article 16 - Equality of opportunity in matters of employment.
 
• The fundamental rights are enshrined in part III of the constitution from Articles 12 to 35.
 
• Part III is described as the Magna Carta of India.
 
• The fundamental rights are guaranteed by the constitution to all persons without any discrimination. 
 
• Features of fundamental rights - 
 
 
• They are justiciable as they are legally enforceable.
 
• They have legal sanctions.
 
• They are automatically enforced. They do not require any legislation for their implementation.
 
• They aim to establish political democracy.
 
• They are negative as they prohibit the state from doing certain things.
 
• They are not absolute but qualified.
 
• They are not permanent.
 
 
 
• The fundamental rights have been taken from the USA i.e., the Bill of Rights.
 
• Originally, the Constitution provided for seven fundamental rights 
 
 
• Right to equality (Articles 14 to 18)
 
• Right to freedom (Articles 19 to 22)
 
• Right against exploitation (Articles 23 to 24)
 
• Right to freedom of religion (Articles 25 to 28)
 
• Cultural and educational rights (Articles 29 to 30)
 
• Right to property (Article 31)
 
• Right to constitutional remedies (Article 32)
 
 
 
• Right to property was deleted by the 44th **Constitutional Amendment Act** of 1978.
 
 
• It is made a legal right under Article 300-A in part XII of the constitution.

questions.question: Which disease is transmitted to humans by a flavivirus that can cause inflammation in the brain?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **__Japanese Encephalitis__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Japanese encephalitis virus causes a brain infection.
 
• Although most illnesses cause little to no symptoms, brain inflammation does occur on occasion. 
 
• Symptoms in these cases can include headache, vomiting, fever, confusion, and seizures. This happens 5 to 15 days after infection.
 
• It is a virus from the** flavivirus **family.
 
• **Flavivirus**
 
 
• Flavivirus, renamed Orthoflavivirus in 2023, is a genus of **positive-strand RNA viruses** in the family Flaviviridae. The genus includes the West Nile virus, dengue virus, tick-borne encephalitis virus, yellow fever virus, Zika virus, and several other viruses which may cause encephalitis, as well as insect-specific flaviviruses (ISFs) such as cell fusing agent virus (CFAV), Palm Creek virus (PCV), and Parramatta River virus (PaRV).
 
 
 
• Japanese encephalitis is the most common form of encephalitis in Southeast Asia.
 
• In the past, outbreaks have occurred in China, Korea, Japan, Taiwan, and Thailand, but the disease has been mostly contained by vaccination. Epidemics also occur on occasion in Vietnam, Cambodia, Myanmar, India, Nepal, and Malaysia.
 
• JEV is primarily transmitted by mosquitos, especially those of the **Culex genus**. As spread through a vector(*Culex *mosquito), it is also called a vector-borne disease. 
 
• Blood or cerebrospinal fluid examination is used to make a diagnosis.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__ **

 
• **Anthrax**

 
 
• Anthrax causes a fatal blood disease known as sorter's disease.
 
• It is a rare infectious disease caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis.
 
• It occurs naturally around the world in wild and domestic hoofed animals, especially cattle, sheep, goats, camels, and antelopes.
 
• It can also occur in humans when they are exposed to the bacterium, usually through handling animals or animals' hides.
 
• There are 3 forms of anthrax infection: cutaneous (skin), inhalation (lungs), and gastrointestinal (stomach and intestine).
 
 
 
• Leptospirosis ​
 
 
• Leptospirosis is caused by bacteria.
 
• It is a zoonotic disease and affects both animals and humans.
 
• It is transmitted by the urine and feces of animals.
 
• The urine-borne disease of rats is Leptospirosis.
 
• It causes fever, chill, vomiting, and diarrhea.
 
• It is treated by taking antibiotics and drinking a lot of water.

• He started his own Kuchipudi Dance Academy in Chennai to teach and promote the dance form.
 
• He received many awards and recognitions for his contribution to the art form, including the Padma Bhushan in 1998.

• Kuchipudi is among one of India's six classical dance forms.
 
• This dance form is a native of the Andhra Pradesh state and is distinct from the other five classical dance forms by incorporating singing.
 
• It first appeared in the 17th century with Sidhyendra Yogi's creation of the dance-drama Bhama Kalapam, which told the tale of Satyabhama, the alluring but envious wife of the Hindu god Krishna.
 
• Holy water is sprinkled and incense is burned before the dance performance starts.
 
• The characters are introduced, the goddesses of knowledge, wealth, and energy are invoked, and songs about each character's role in the play are played.

• Agnivastra, also known as Bagalbandi, calls for a male dancer to dress in a dhoti (a single pleated piece of cloth hanging down from the waist).
 
• Saris and minimal makeup would be worn by a dancer playing a female role.
 
• The dance-drama performance known as Kuchipudi has its origins in the Natya Shastra, an old Hindu text written in Sanskrit.

questions.question: Which of the following is a secondary function of money?

options.text: Helping in conducting transactions in an economy
Calculating relative prices of goods and services
Being a standard of deferred payments
Allowing purchase and sale to be conducted independently

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **__Being a standard of deferred payments__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Functions of Money:

 
 
• The functions of money are divided into two categories: Primary Functions and Secondary Functions.
 
 
 
• Primary Functions:
 
 
• Medium of Exchange:
 
 
• ​It refers to a monetary function in which money is viewed as a means of exchanging goods.
 
• The medium of exchange function is regarded as the primary and unique function of money because it solved the primary problem of the barter system of double coincident wants.
 
 
 
• Measure of Value:
 
 
• ​It refers to a monetary function that aids in determining the value of goods and services. The value of all goods and services is expressed in terms of money.
 
• When calculating the monetary value of goods and services, money is used as the common denominator.
 
 
 
 
 
• Secondary Functions:
 
 
• Store of Value:
 
 
• Individuals typically keep their wealth in the form of money. As a result, money functions as an asset that retains its value over time.
 
 
 
• Standard of Deferred Payments:
 
 
• ​It refers to one of the money's most important functions. Loans, salaries, pensions, insurance premiums, interest, and rents are examples of deferred payments.
 
• The amount of repaid money must be the same as it was at the time of purchase, which is a necessary condition for deferred payment.
 
 
 
• Transfer of Value:
 
 
• ​Money's utility extends to the transfer of value because it can be used to purchase goods not only within the country but also beyond its borders.
 
• Money as a standard tool can be used to sell or buy goods in the domestic or international market.

questions.question: Where did Lord Wavell call a conference between Congress and Muslim League leaders to reach an agreement?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **__Simla__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Shimla Conference

 
 
• A conference of 21 Indian political leaders was invited to Shimla, the summer capital of the British Government, to discuss the provisions of the Wavell Plan.
 
• Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, the President of the Congress at the time, was among the leaders. Mohammad Ali Jinnah was also present at the conference.
 
• Convened to agree on and approve the Wavell Plan for Indian self-government, it reached a potential agreement for Indian self-rule that provided Muslims with separate representation and reduced majority powers for both communities in their majority regions.
 
• However, talks came to a halt over the issue of selecting Muslim representatives.
 
• Jinnah stated that no non-league Muslim should be represented on the Executive Council because only the Muslim League has the authority to represent Indian Muslims.
 
• Jinnah also demanded that if votes were divided and Muslim members objected, a provision be added requiring a two-thirds majority to clear a vote.
 
• Wavell had appointed six Muslims to the Executive Council of 14, and the British had given it the power to veto any constitutional proposal that was not in its best interests.
 
• However, Muslims made up only 25% of the Indian population. As a result, Congress rejected these unreasonable demands.
 
• The Muslim League refused to back down, and Wavell scrapped the plan.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Wavell Plan was initially introduced in 1945 at the Shimla Conference. It was named after Lord Wavell, Viceroy of India.
 
• The Shimla Conference was held in order to reach an agreement on the Wavell Plan for Indian self-government, which called for separate representation on communal lines.
 
• The failure of both the plan and the conference was due to the failure of the Muslim League and the Indian National Congress to reach an agreement.
 
• Proposals for the Wavell Plan
 
 
• All members of the executive council, with the exception of the governor-general and the commander-in-chief, were to be Indians.
 
• Caste Hindus and Muslims were to be represented equally.
 
• The reconstructed council was to function as an interim government within the framework of the 1935 Act (i.e., not accountable to the Central Assembly).
 
• The governor-general was to exercise his veto on ministerial advice.
 
• Representatives from various parties were to submit a joint list to the viceroy for nominations to the executive council.
 
• If a joint list was not possible, separate lists were to be submitted, with the possibility of negotiations on a new constitution being kept open once the war was won.
 
• The Scheduled Castes would also be represented separately, and the possibility of a new constitution would be discussed.
 
• The Governor-Veto General's would not be abolished, but it would not be used excessively.
 
• The Governor-General's portfolio of external affairs was to be transferred to an Indian member of the Council.
 
• It was also expected that "provincial ministers in the province would return to office and that a coalition would form."
 
• Congress leaders were allowed to attend the Simla Conference in June 1945. This marked the end of a period of confrontation that had lasted since August 1942.
